newsitem.title: CHINA: Tibet leader accuses Westerners of Tibet collusion.
newsitem.headline: Tibet leader accuses Westerners of Tibet collusion.

text.p: A senior Tibetan leader on Friday accused Western nations of colluding with pro-independence activists who launched a wave of bombings and acts of sabotage in the restive Himalayan region last year.

Separatists backed by hostile foreign forces and followers of the exiled spiritual leader the Dalai Lama had adopted new methods in their fight to shake off Beijing rule, said Raidi, chairman of the Tibetan People's Congress.
"In recent years... the separatism has changed somewhat, some terrorists have used all kinds of methods to engage in sabotage activities," he told a news conference in Beijing.
"This cannot be separated from collusion at home and abroad," he said. "The Dalai Lama clique... enemy Western forces.. Western countries, they are all there."
Tibet remained stable, despite separatist attacks that included a wave of bombings and assassinations, he said.
Fears of unrest among China's ethnic minorities have risen in recent months, fueled by reports of ethnic violence both in Tibet and the neighbouring far-western region of Xinjiang.
Exiled Uighur nationalists have claimed responsibility for bomb attacks in mainly-Moslem Xinjiang last week that killed at least nine people and wounded 74.

Three bombs planted on buses blew up within minutes of each other in the regional capital Urumqi on February 25 in an attack apparently timed to coincide with funeral rites in Beijing for paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.
The blasts came two months after a Christmas Day bombing in the Tibetan capital Lhasa that prompted tightened security across the mountainous region.
Conditions in Tibet and Xinjiang were very different and most people in both regions opposed all attempts to divide the Chinese motherland, said Raidi, himself an ethnic Tibetan.

Chinese officials have said the Lhasa blast was politically motivated and carried out by followers of the Dalai Lama, who is still revered in the deeply-Buddhist region decades after fleeing into exile following an abortive uprising in 1959.

Tibet's government-in-exile in India has dismissed suggestions the bombing was carried out by supporters of the Dalai Lama, who in 1989 won the Nobel Peace Prize for his non-violent campaign for Tibetan autonomy.
"Western forces consider the Dalai Lama as an important tool, so they use him to carry out sabotage," said Raidi.
The chairman, in Beijing to represent Tibet at the annual session of China's National People's Congress, also took aim at Taiwan for its plans to welcome the Dalai Lama this month.
China has condemned the six-day visit and has warned Taipei not to fan separatist sentiment while the Dalai Lama is on the island, which Beijing considers a rebel province.
"Tibet and Taiwan are both inseparable parts of the Chinese nation and are both inseparable parts of Chinese territory," Raidi said. "We resolutely oppose all separatist activities."
He was less forthcoming when asked about the whereabouts of the boy chosen by the Dalai Lama as the reincarnated "soul boy" of the late 10th Panchen Lama, Tibet's second holiest monk.

Western human rights groups have accused China of detaining Gedhun Choekyi Nyima after choosing another child to be the 11th Panchen Lama, but Raidi said the seven-year-old was free, living well and with his parents.
But he steered clear of specifics on the boy's location.
"He is within the territory of the People's Republic of China," he said.
